If Jonas gained confidence, then (overcomes fears ∨ takes risks) would be true.
But both disjuncts are false in the context; hence by modus tollens Jonas cannot gain confidence.

Therefore the disjunction “develops a unique style ∨ gains confidence” is false, contradicting what the dedication rule requires.

Thus the assumption “Jonas is dedicated to his craft” leads to a contradiction with the rest of the context. In classical entailment, if assuming the antecedent produces a contradiction, the conditional “If Jonas is dedicated to his craft, then …” is vacuously true: there is no consistent situation in which the antecedent holds and the consequent fails, because the antecedent cannot hold at all. Hence the statement is entailed.
